analysis.one_liner: Makes failed-bank executives repay up to five years of pay and holds parent companies liable for bailout costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote; it was referred to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended, despite 5 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails and the FDIC takes it over, this bill would require the FDIC to take back up to five years of compensation — salary, bonuses, stock awards, and stock-trading profits — from executives who were substantially responsible for the failure. The recovered money would go into the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Treasury. It would also make a failed bank's holding company liable to the FDIC for payments made to insured depositors, the FDIC's costs as receiver, and interest, with first claim on the holding company's assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers and taxpayers benefit. When a bank fails, the FDIC pays insured depositors out of the Deposit Insurance Fund, which is funded by bank fees — and uninsured depositors or the public can end up backstopping losses in large failures. Clawing back executive pay after a failure shifts losses onto the people who caused them instead of the insurance fund, and holding the parent company liable gives the FDIC a stronger claim to recover bailout costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDIC to claw back all or part of five years of compensation — salary, bonuses, performance and equity awards, and stock-trading profits — from executives substantially responsible for a failed bank, with the money deposited into the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Treasury.

Makes a failed bank's holding company liable to the FDIC for payments to insured depositors, receiver costs, and interest, secured by an automatic lien on all holding-company assets with payment priority over other creditors and shareholders.
Applies the same clawback to large 'covered financial companies' resolved under the Dodd-Frank orderly liquidation process, not just smaller insured banks.

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failed banks, who could lose up to five years of pay after a failure they were substantially responsible for, and bank holding companies, which would face direct liability for the FDIC's payout and receiver costs with a priority lien on their assets. Banks generally could also face higher compliance and legal costs.

drawbacks.text: The 'substantially responsible' standard gives the FDIC judgment over which executives must repay compensation, and a mandated five-year lookback could capture executives whose role in a failure was minor or who left the bank long before it collapsed, inviting litigation and claims of unfairness.

Making holding companies unconditionally liable for all FDIC payments with priority over every other creditor goes well beyond executive pay and could make bank parent companies riskier or more expensive to finance, effects the bill's sponsors did not address in the text.
Stronger executive liability could make it harder for banks to recruit and retain senior executives, a cost banks regularly argue accompanies clawback rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that executives who run a bank into failure should bear some of the losses they caused, rather than leaving them on the deposit insurance fund — is a straightforward accountability measure, and it attracted support from both parties in the aftermath of the 2023 bank failures. The clawback structure (an FDIC judgment call on fault, a five-year lookback) and the broad holding-company liability provision are blunt instruments that could produce unfair results or litigation, but those are design problems, not reasons the outcome served the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, months after the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank put the cost of bank rescues in the headlines.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
It had 4 cosponsors split evenly between the parties — two Republicans and two Democrats — but bipartisan sponsorship never translated into committee action.
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Failed-bank executives and bank holding companies are better off: no clawback of compensation was ever enacted, and holding companies never faced the new liability to the FDIC for depositor payouts and receivership costs. The Deposit Insurance Fund and the public never gained the recovery mechanism.

industries.industry: Bank executives and bank holding companies
industries.note: Executives at failed banks would repay up to five years of compensation, and holding companies would become directly liable for the FDIC's depositor payouts and receivership costs with first claim on their assets. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs directly against depositors and the insurance fund that otherwise absorb the losses.

Healthy banks fund the Deposit Insurance Fund through premiums, so recovering losses from failed-bank executives would ease pressure on the fund and could lower premium costs over time — though banks also argued stricter liability rules raise compliance and financing costs.

industries.industry: FDIC and the Deposit Insurance Fund
industries.note: The FDIC would gain a mandatory clawback tool and a priority claim against holding companies, replenishing the fund that protects ordinary depositors.
